overview: The Indus, or Harappan, civilization connected cities, villages and workshops across present-day Pakistan and northwestern India. Its major urban phase flourished around 2600 to 1900 BCE. The map reuses a broad outline from 4000 to 1500 BCE: this is an approximate cultural region, not verified borders of one empire. Its early start does not mean all the famous cities already existed.

periods.title: Earlier regional communities
periods.summary: Farming settlements and craft networks preceded the mature cities; this starts at the map’s early coverage, not a founding event.

periods.title: The mature urban phase
periods.summary: Large cities, planned neighborhoods and long-distance exchange flourished.

periods.title: Transformation after the urban peak
periods.summary: Settlements and production changed, while communities continued beyond this map’s endpoint.

sections.title: Cities and the work of living together

items.text: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa belonged to a wider network of large towns and smaller settlements. Their planned street layouts and shared craft traditions show substantial coordination. Connections also stretched westward through trade. The familiar label “civilization” describes these linked communities; it does not give us the name of a securely identified emperor.

Dholavira stood on dry Khadir island in present-day Gujarat. Two seasonal streams supplied an ingenious system of water storage, with reservoirs beside its elevated central area. Much of the city was built in stone. Here, planning for the dry season shaped the whole settlement, rather than being a household chore left until the last jar was empty.

Dholavira’s houses differed in size and construction quality, and its residential areas were divided by substantial walls. Archaeologists interpret these contrasts as signs of social differences. Shared engineering did not mean everyone enjoyed an identical home. Excavated workshops and ornaments also connect this regional center with other Harappan cities, Oman and Mesopotamia.

At Dholavira, most structures in the cemetery were memorials rather than graves containing bodies. Their varied forms show that remembering the dead could involve building a monument without putting a person beneath it. Archaeologists therefore have to distinguish a place of commemoration from a burial before asking what it says about family or belief.

Excavators at Harappa identified toilets made from large jars sunk into floors, sometimes with a smaller washing jar inside. Some drained into channels; others let liquid seep through a small bottom opening. Sand was spread on toilet floors, which were renewed from time to time. Ingenious plumbing still left someone with the cleaning. These examples do not mean every household had the same facilities.

Harappa’s clay carts could be tiny enough for play. Daya Ram Sahni’s 1921 excavation report describes a shallow cart body with side rings for an axle and a front ring for a pulling string. Separate clay wheels also survived. The interpretation as a toy turns these small finds into a particularly appealing glimpse of childhood: a miniature version of grown-up transport.

A small clay bed from Harappa preserves the impression of finely woven cloth. Its evenly spun threads and close weave date to the Harappan phase, around 2600 to 1900 BCE. The cloth itself has disappeared, but its pattern remained pressed into the clay. An object that looks like a toy can therefore preserve evidence of someone else’s careful spinning and weaving.

Cooking pots can retain microscopic traces of meals. A study of vessels from towns and villages in northwestern India found residues consistent with animal fats and some dairy products. Mixtures of ingredients make exact identification difficult, so these are clues rather than complete menus. Similar products appeared in rural and urban vessels, and some cooking practices continued after the major cities declined.

At Chanhudaro, the same bead workshop made roughly finished short beads and beautifully polished long carnelian beads. The simpler pieces had holes pecked through them; the elaborate ones required specialized stone drills. Different finishes need not mean different centuries or different towns. One workshop could supply several kinds of ornament, and an unfinished or unworn bead can reveal how the work was done.

Cube-shaped weights from Harappa and Allahdino followed a series that doubled: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. A common weight was about 13.7 grams. Combining small weights let people compare quantities of goods. The practical arithmetic is recognizable even without reading an inscription: if one weight is not enough, try a larger one or add another.

Harappa’s burial evidence offers a less comfortable side of city life. Researchers found bone changes consistent with infections, including leprosy and tuberculosis, in some individuals from urban and later burial areas. The remains are fragmentary, and different groups did not show equal risks. Well-planned drains were an achievement, but they did not make everyone healthy or reveal which treatments people tried.

sections.title: Writing that we cannot yet read

items.text: A real sample survives on British Museum seal 1947,0416.1 from Mohenjo-daro: five signs carved above a standing bull. The steatite object is only 3.7 centimeters square and dates to about 2600 to 1900 BCE. Its inscription belongs to the still-undeciphered Indus script. We can identify the surviving marks, but cannot honestly provide their spoken wording or translation. The museum’s object record shows the original witness.

A study of river landscapes connects the urban transformation with weakening monsoon rains and less dependable flooding. Farming communities adapted by changing crops and shifting settlement toward areas with more reliable water. Climate was one pressure within a complicated social history. The evidence describes changes unfolding across a region, rather than a single terrible afternoon when an entire civilization vanished.

At Harappa, an unfinished carnelian bead from a pot dated around 1700 BCE has a hole made with a tubular drill. Researchers take it as evidence that ornament workshops still operated after the great urban phase, using a changed technique. A city could shrink and trade networks could alter while somebody was still at a workbench, trying to finish a bead.

ending.text: After about 1900 BCE, many large urban centers contracted and settlement patterns changed. Environmental pressures, disrupted exchange and social inequalities formed part of this transformation; their relative importance remains debated. People continued farming, cooking and making things in smaller settlements and surviving towns. The map’s 1500 BCE endpoint is not a disappearance date for the population or all Harappan traditions.
